title: Effectiveness of virtual reality (VR)-based social skills training (VR-SST) compared to VR-based resource activation (VR-RA) for children with aggressive behavior toward peers
summary:
As part of social skills training programs for children with disruptive behavior disorders  (DBD), role-playing is among the standard psychotherapeutic methods used. However, not all affected children benefit equally from conventional interventions. One possible reason is that challenging situations from a child’s everyday life can be difficult to address within therapy sessions, e.g., conflict situations.

VIT4Kids is a program developed to help close these gaps by integrating virtual reality (VR) into psychotherapy. VR enables children to interact with age-appropriate virtual characters in a child-friendly virtual environment, thereby creating a new approach to psychotherapy. The study described here is suitable for children who frequently experience conflicts with peers and who display verbal and/or physical aggressive behavior in these situations.
The VIT4Kids project currently consists of two interventions: 1) VR-based Social Skills Training (VR-SST), which aims to improve children’s problem-solving skills; 2) VR-based Resource Activation (VR-RA), which seeks to enhance children’s self-esteem by increasing awareness of their personal strengths.
Within this study, the effectiveness of twelve sessions of VR-SST will be compared with twelve sessions of VR-RA. Both interventions will be examined with regard to various scientific research questions.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Diagnosis of Conduct Disorder (F91.X ), Hyperkinetic Conduct Disorder (F90.1 ), Combined Disorder of Conduct and Emotions (F92); elevated scores of peer-related aggression in parent-rating.
Exclusion criteria:
Diagnosis of a pervasive developmental disorder (F84) or another mental disorder; acute crisis-related escalation of problematic behavior such that inpatient treatment would be indicated; IQ below 80 on the Culture Fair Test; indications of epilepsy in the past or present; occurrence of cybersickness during the VR introductory session
